titel: Goals and instruments of central banks
kurz: A central bank directly sets only a single price and depends on banks and markets to pass it on to the rest of the economy.

bloecke.md:
A central bank produces nothing and sells nothing, and measured against its impact it has only a few employees. It directly determines only a single price, the overnight interest rate for central bank money. Everything else (mortgage rates, rates on instant-access savings accounts, equity valuations and the external value of the euro) only follows from this via markets and expectations and with a time lag. When judging monetary policy, you therefore have to separate the question of which goal the central bank is allowed to pursue at all from the question of the chain through which its decision takes effect.

## Mandates and reaction functions

The ECB has a **hierarchical mandate**. Article 127 TFEU (Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union) names price stability as the primary objective. The Eurosystem may support the Union's general economic policies only insofar as this is possible without prejudice to this objective. For the ECB, employment is a piece of information and not a mandate in its own right. The Federal Reserve works with a **dual mandate**, in which maximum employment and stable prices stand side by side with equal weight. The statute also names moderate long-term interest rates as a rarely cited third element. Both central banks have put a number on their price target. Since the 2021 strategy review, the ECB has aimed symmetrically for an inflation rate of 2% over the medium term as measured by the HICP (Harmonised Index of Consumer Prices), and the Fed for 2% as measured by the PCE price index over the longer run.

bloecke.md:
The difference becomes apparent when a supply shock means that the two goals call for different responses. That was the case in 2026, when rising energy prices pushed up headline inflation while domestic price pressure remained comparatively low. In Germany the inflation rate was 2.9% in August 2026, whereas the core rate excluding energy and food was 2.4%. Energy alone became 10.5% more expensive, fuels 27.7%. In the USA the headline rate in the same month was 3.4% and the core rate 2.4%, with an unemployment rate of 4.1%.

For the Fed this creates a conflict of objectives, because tightening against an imported price shock costs jobs that the law requires it to protect. Formally, the ECB does not have to make this trade-off, but in practice it does, because the road to price stability runs through the economy. Despite their different mandates, both central banks acted in the same way in September 2026. On 10 September the ECB raised all three key interest rates by 25 basis points, effective from 16 September. On 16 September the Fed unanimously raised its target range for the first time since 2023, to 3.75-4.00%, effective from 17 September.

bloecke.md:
## The deposit facility rate as the de facto key interest rate

In the textbook, a central bank steers the money market through its weekly refinancing operations. Banks bid for a scarce quantity of reserves, and the main refinancing rate is the decisive price. This procedure ended in October 2008, when the ECB switched to fixed-rate tenders with **full allotment**. Since then, every bank has received as much central bank money as it wants against adequate collateral. In addition, there was the [[excess liquidity]] from the bond purchases. In mid-2026 there were still around €2,161 billion of excess reserves in the system. Banks with ample reserves do not need to borrow money. Instead, they look for the best investment for their balances, and the deposit facility offers it. The money market rate therefore lies at the lower edge of the interest rate corridor and not in its middle.

Since 18 September 2024 the spread between the main refinancing rate and the deposit facility rate has been narrowed to 15 basis points. With this, the ECB is preparing for the case that excess liquidity continues to fall and banks at some point have to refinance themselves actively again. The aim is to keep the money market rate from jumping during the transition.

bloecke.titel: ECB deposit facility rate and upper bound of the Fed target range since 2007
bloecke.unter: The chart shows two decades of interest rate policy, with the sharp rate cuts of 2008, eight years of negative rates in the euro area, the steepest tightening cycle in decades in 2022/23 and the reversal in 2026, in June at the ECB and in September at the Fed.

bloecke.md: Between June 2003 and December 2005 and between May 2009 and April 2011, the ECB left its key interest rates unchanged. The Fed's key rate was practically zero from December 2008 to December 2015 and again from March 2020 to March 2022, around nine of eighteen years in total. Key interest rates often stay at one level for a long time; turning points are rare and then often happen quickly. Planning for a portfolio or for follow-up financing that assumes steady small rate steps contradicts this historical pattern.

## The balance sheet as a second instrument

At the lower bound on interest rates, the key interest rate cannot be cut any further. The central bank then buys bonds, that is, it takes securities out of the market and pays for them with central bank reserves. This lowers long-term interest rates and risk premiums. This approach is called **quantitative easing** (QE). In the reverse process, **quantitative tightening** (QT), maturing securities are no longer replaced, and the balance sheet shrinks passively.

Stock and flow have to be distinguished. The effect of QE depends on the stock held and not on the monthly pace of purchases. A central bank that stops buying is therefore a long way from tightening, and a central bank that shrinks its balance sheet does not reverse QE point for point.

bloecke.titel: Total assets of the Eurosystem and the Federal Reserve since 2007
bloecke.unter: Values at the start of each year, last point September 2026. The Eurosystem is shown in € billion and the Fed in $ billion, without currency conversion, because what matters is the shape of the curves.

bloecke.md:
At the start of 2007, the Eurosystem managed with total assets of €1,154 billion. On 24 June 2022 the balance sheet reached its peak of €8,836 billion, and on 11 September 2026 it stood at €5,911 billion. Around €2,925 billion has thus been run down, or about 38% of the increase from the pre-crisis level to the peak. Even so, the balance sheet is still just over five times as large as in 2007.

The Fed's balance sheet stood at around $870 billion in August 2007, reached its peak of $8,965 billion on 13 April 2022 and stands at $6,747 billion on 16 September 2026. It already reached its low of $6,536 billion on 3 December 2025, and it has been growing again since then. The Fed's QT has therefore ended, while it continues in the euro area. There, excess liquidity fell by around a further €55 billion in the reporting period.

The Fed is thus tightening its monetary policy via the interest rate while enlarging its balance sheet at the same time. This is not a contradiction, because the two instruments have different tasks. The interest rate steers demand, while the size of the balance sheet mainly governs how well the banking system is supplied with reserves.

In a bond purchase, the central bank swaps a security for central bank reserves. Reserves circulate between the banks and the central bank. They do not land directly in current accounts and are not spent on purchases. The Fed almost quintupled its balance sheet from the pre-crisis level of 2007 to the start of 2020 without inflation reaching its target on a lasting basis. Conversely, it does not follow that QE has no effect. It changes asset prices, risk appetite and the government's financing costs, though not through a fixed mechanism by which a larger money supply automatically means higher prices.

## Expectations as an instrument

Because monetary policy works through markets, its effect begins as soon as markets expect a decision, and not only when the central bank acts. This is the basis of **forward guidance**. A central bank commits itself to a future path of interest rates in order to lower today's long-term rates without spending any money today. The best-known example of the effect of such an announcement cost the central bank no money.

bloecke.text: ready to do whatever it takes to preserve the euro
bloecke.quelle: Mario Draghi, Global Investment Conference, London, 26 July 2012

bloecke.md:
Spreads fell before a single euro had been spent on the announced programme. The effect rested solely on the credibility of the announcement.

Such a commitment becomes a drawback when the situation changes. Pledges not to raise interest rates “for an extended period” came into conflict with the surge in inflation in 2021/22. The ECB therefore abandoned its date-based and state-based advance commitments and has since explicitly taken its decisions meeting by meeting, depending on the data. This is more honest, but it makes monetary policy harder to predict. A central bank that does not commit itself loses influence over expectations.

bloecke.titel: Transmission mechanism from the overnight rate to consumer prices
bloecke.unter: On the left are the central bank's instruments, on the right the variables it wants to influence, and in between lie markets that it does not control.

bloecke.md: The ECB itself describes the lags in this chain as long, variable and uncertain. A central bank therefore bases its decisions on the forecast and not on the current inflation rate. Interest rate decisions consequently cannot be meaningfully judged by the previous month's inflation rate. The projection of 10 September 2026 follows this reasoning and does not foresee a return to target until 2028.

bloecke.md:
## Key interest rate and market rates

The key interest rate is an overnight rate for banks. The yields on long-term bonds are formed in the market from expectations about inflation, growth and risk, and these expectations can develop differently from what the central bank is aiming for. This was particularly evident in 2026. With a deposit facility rate of 2.50%, the yield on ten-year German federal bonds (Bunds) rose from an August average of 3.18% to around 3.5% in mid-September, its highest level since 2011. The ten-year US yield reached 5.01% on 16 September, a level last seen in 2007. Mortgage rates are based on Pfandbriefe (German covered bonds) and Bunds and not on the key interest rate. They can therefore rise while the ECB is cutting rates.

bloecke.md:
## Independence and its rationale

Central bank independence is the answer to a specific incentive problem, **time inconsistency**. A government that controls the money supply itself always has a short-term reason to allow a little more inflation. More inflation reduces the real value of debt and stimulates the economy before an election, while the rise in prices only follows later. Citizens, companies and markets know about this incentive and price it in. The result is higher inflation without the hoped-for gain in employment. The way out is to hand the decision to an institution with a narrow mandate, long terms of office and freedom from instructions. In the euro area this is secured twice over in the Treaty. Article 130 TFEU prohibits instructions to the ECB, and Article 123 TFEU prohibits the direct financing of governments by the central bank.

There is empirical evidence for this argument, but it is weaker than it is often made out to be. In post-war comparisons, countries with independent central banks had lower inflation on average, without having to accept lower growth in return. The causality is disputed, however. Societies that already place a high value on stable money also tend to create independent central banks. The institution could therefore be a consequence just as much as a cause. Germany with its Bundesbank is considered the most important example for both readings.

Independence also does not mean freedom from oversight. In return, the legislature sets a narrow objective for which the central bank has to account, in hearings at the European Parliament, in semi-annual reports to the US Congress and through published projections and minutes. This commitment to a narrow objective is what the current dispute is about. According to one view, a central bank that pursues distributional or climate goals at its own discretion leaves the mandate that justifies its independence in the first place. According to the other, such risks affect price stability and financial stability anyway, through loan defaults and supply shocks, and therefore belong in the mandate. Both positions are defensible within the legal framework, and the dispute has not been settled.

Political pressure on central banks has historically been the norm. Whether it is having an effect shows up in the inflation rate only late. It can be recognised earlier from two variables: long-term inflation expectations (so far anchored at around 2% in the euro area) and the long end of the yield curve. If long-term yields rise while the central bank is easing, the market is demanding a premium for future currency depreciation. Such a rise expresses distrust of the central bank and is not a signal about the economy.

- The key interest rate is not the rate on your own account. Rates on instant-access savings accounts follow the deposit facility rate with a delay and only partly; the competitive pressure on the bank also plays a part.
- For mortgage financing, what counts are the yields on Bunds and Pfandbriefe, not the ECB press conference.
- It is worth calculating the real interest rate. With a deposit facility rate of 2.50% and inflation of 3.3% in Germany, the short-term real interest rate in September 2026 is negative, so balances lose purchasing power despite positive interest rates.
- Projections say more than headlines. A central bank's reaction function shows in its forecasts, not in the previous month's inflation figure.

bloecke.titel: Negative rates and the lower bound
bloecke.md: From June 2014 to July 2022 the ECB deposit facility rate was negative, at its lowest from September 2019 at -0.50%. During these eight years, banks paid for their excess reserves. A negative interest rate is only possible because cash, while offering an interest rate of zero, involves costs for storage, insurance and transport. Only when the negative rate exceeds these costs does switching to cash pay off. This threshold is known as the effective lower bound, and it lies slightly below zero. Banks mostly did not pass the negative rate on to retail customers because they feared deposit outflows. This shows that the transmission of monetary policy can be interrupted at any stage of the chain.

mitnehmen: A central bank directly sets only one price, the overnight rate for central bank money; in the Eurosystem, with full allotment since October 2008 and the excess liquidity, that is de facto the deposit facility rate and not the main refinancing rate, and since March 2024 it has also been so explicitly.
The ECB has a hierarchical mandate with priority for price stability, the Fed a dual mandate with employment given equal weight, and this difference matters above all in supply shocks.
Bond purchases work through the stock held and not through the pace of buying; the Fed already ended its QT in December 2025, while the Eurosystem is still shrinking its balance sheet.
Because interest rate decisions work with long, variable and uncertain lags, a central bank is guided by the forecast and not by the current inflation figure.

Central bank independence solves the time inconsistency problem and in return requires a narrow mandate; empirically it goes hand in hand with lower inflation, but the direction of causality is disputed.

Since 16 September 2026 it has stood at 2.50%.

Band formed by the marginal lending facility rate (top), the main refinancing rate (middle) and the deposit facility rate (bottom), within which the money market rate moves. Banks' central bank balances to the extent that they exceed minimum reserves. In the euro area, excess liquidity stood at around €2,161 billion in mid-2026, and it is falling because monetary policy securities holdings are running off.

Reduction of a central bank's securities holdings, usually passively, by not reinvesting maturing securities. QT works through the stock held and not through the pace, and it does not reverse previous purchases point for point.

A binding or conditional statement by a central bank about its future interest rate path. It lowers today's long-term interest rates without deploying money, but costs credibility if the pledge later has to be broken.

A government's incentive to allow more inflation in the short term even though it promises price stability in the long term. Because markets price in this incentive, the result is higher inflation without any gain in employment. Time inconsistency is the most important rationale for central bank independence.
